title: Guru Amar Das close
hook: humility, equality, and a kitchen open to all

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns of the mind: O restless mind, no one finds Him through cleverness. Your line was rest in the word. Which line did you rest in? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

Steam rising off big pots. Someone stirring dal with a paddle as long as an arm. Rows of people on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and a volunteer coming down the line with a bucket of rotis, handing one to each open palm. It doesn't matter who's sitting there. A farmer, a banker, a stranger who wandered in. Same floor, same food, same hands serving it. That kitchen is where we end our time with Guru Amar Das, because the hymns of the past days show up in it, cooked down to something you can eat.
screen: `STEAM, DAL, A LONG PADDLE.` → `SAME FLOOR, SAME FOOD.` → `THE HYMNS, COOKED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Three threads run through his time, and the kitchen ties them together. Humility. Tradition remembers him as a servant long before anyone called him Guru, carrying water in the dark. His hymns warn again and again about haumai, ego, and say ego and the Name can't share one room. In the langar, nobody eats in a place of honor; everyone sits on the same floor. Equality. Tradition remembers his well at Goindval as open to every caste, his teachers on their manjis as women and men, and his voice against a tax on pilgrims. He took the word sati off the pyre and gave it to faithful lives. In the langar, nobody is asked who their family is before the roti is handed over. And a kitchen open to all. Sikh tradition gives Guru Amar Das a large part in making the langar central, so that those who came to see the Guru sat in the row and ate first. The meal itself became a teaching about who belongs. Put the pieces together and you can hear the old Guru's voice in the clatter of the pots. O mind, you are the form of light, and so, in the Sikh view, is the person beside you. The world is burning, so feed whoever comes, by any door. Face the Guru, not only yourself. Let ego die a little in the serving. And when the mind is restless, rest in the Word, then pick up the bucket and walk the row. That's Guru Amar Das, closed for now. Tomorrow, his successor, Guru Ram Das, and the shape of a Sikh's morning.
screen: `HUMILITY: THE WATER CARRIER.` · `EQUALITY: THE WELL, THE MANJIS, THE PYRE.` · `THE ROW BEFORE THE AUDIENCE.` · `THE HYMNS IN THE CLATTER OF POTS.` · then, large: `OPEN KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open your door once. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own kitchen, or your table, or just your free hour this week. Now picture the door to it. Who usually comes through, and who never does? Let one person come to mind who could use a seat: a neighbor, a new coworker, someone alone. Picture them sitting down, and something simple being handed to them. No grand plan. Just the door, opening. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Guru Amar Das close. Humility, equality and a kitchen open to all: the old Guru's hymns of ego, light and the Word, cooked down into a shared meal. Today's word.

Your line: open kitchen. This week, invite the person you thought of to share something, a meal, a coffee, a seat at your table, and let them in without any test. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and serve and everyone sits together on the floor or at shared tables; Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's part in it, along with his hymns, on his gurpurab.
